cards.title: Choose CRO strategy by monthly session volume
cards.summary: Use large structural changes below roughly 300,000 monthly sessions and a comprehensive AB-testing program only when traffic can support it.
cards.use_when: Allocating a store's CRO resources between major redesigns, offer tests, and isolated experiments.
steps: Pull monthly sessions and order volume from analytics before choosing a testing model.

Treat roughly 300,000 monthly sessions as the source's directional dividing line, not a universal rule. Below it, prioritize big swings: data-informed PDP redesigns, distinct landing-page concepts, and offer or price changes.

Above it, if the store also has sufficient orders and a viable conversion rate, invest in comprehensive CRO: audits, quantitative and qualitative research, data analysis, prioritized hypotheses, and isolated AB tests.

Check practical test power rather than relying on the traffic threshold alone. If an isolated change cannot receive enough sample, test a larger concept or consolidate changes into a deliberate structural variation.
caveats: The source does not define a minimum conversion rate, order count, or testable effect size.
The 300,000-session line is a source heuristic that the presenter says has changed over time; recalculate feasibility for the individual store.

cards.title: Use big swings rather than micro-tests on low-traffic stores
cards.summary: When a store lacks volume for element-level tests, use research-led PDP, landing-page, offer, and pricing concepts that can create a meaningful revenue-per-visitor shift.
cards.use_when: Building a CRO roadmap for a lower-traffic store that cannot reliably power button-color, small-copy, or image-swap experiments.
steps: Avoid spending the roadmap on isolated, low-impact page elements when traffic makes them slow or underpowered.
Start with evidence: inspect funnel drop-off and heatmaps, then collect survey and interview feedback to identify the shopper problem a larger redesign should solve.
Build substantial variants such as a PDP redesign, a different paid-traffic landing-page concept, a bundle page, or a materially different offer or price point.
Evaluate the change by revenue per visitor or session, since an offer or redesign can affect both purchase conversion and average order value.
Use the outcome to decide whether to retain the new concept and identify the next structural bottleneck; do not assume a dramatic result merely because the change is large.
caveats: The source advocates data-based redesigns but does not prescribe what every PDP redesign must include.
Claims that large changes can double conversion or revenue per session are presented rhetorically rather than as a general performance expectation.

cards.title: Route paid traffic through a pre-sell landing page
cards.summary: Use a dedicated landing page between an ad click and a PDP or collection page to establish the angle and offer before shoppers reach the buying page.
cards.use_when: Improving paid-acquisition journeys that currently send cold traffic directly to a homepage, collection, or product page.
steps: Map the current paid path from ad click to product page, cart, checkout, and purchase to establish revenue per visitor and downstream conversion.
Create a dedicated pre-sell landing page before the PDP or collection page. Give it a specific audience angle and offer rather than using a generic storefront page.
Use the page to prepare shoppers for the product and the next action, then direct qualified visitors to the relevant product or collection page.

Measure the full journey, including landing-page visitors, product-page progression, purchase conversion, average order value, and revenue per visitor. Do not judge the page solely by its click-through rate.
Treat the landing page as a larger concept to test, especially where low traffic makes micro-tests impractical.
caveats: The source does not specify required landing-page sections, length, or offer mechanics.
A source example of cold-traffic revenue and scalable spend is an illustration, not a benchmark or promised outcome.

cards.title: Test offers and price points on a monthly cadence
cards.summary: Use recurring offer and pricing experiments, including bundles and multi-buy promotions, and judge them on revenue per visitor rather than conversion rate alone.
cards.use_when: Seeking a high-impact merchandising lever for product pricing, bundles, or promotions without depending on fine-grained page tests.
steps: Maintain a recurring cadence for testing offers rather than treating the current discount, bundle, or price as permanent.
Create materially different offer structures such as buy-one-get-one, three-for-the-price-of-two, or a build-a-bundle page.
Test alternative price points directly where commercially appropriate.
Keep the offer hypothesis distinct from layout changes where possible, so the business can attribute performance to the commercial proposition rather than a mixed redesign.
Assess purchase conversion, average order value, gross margin, and revenue per visitor or session. A promotion that raises conversion but reduces revenue per visitor is not automatically a winner.
Document the audience, traffic source, and duration so a seasonal or channel-specific result is not applied indiscriminately.
caveats: The source provides no test duration, sample-size requirement, or winner threshold for offers.
The source wording for a three-item promotion appears transcription-ambiguous; validate the exact offer structure before publishing it.

cards.title: Remove an unused discount-code field from cart
cards.summary: When no promotion is active, remove a visible discount field that can prompt shoppers to leave checkout to search for coupon codes.
cards.use_when: Auditing cart or checkout friction on a store that shows a promo-code field despite having no active discount.
steps: Inspect the cart and checkout experience for a discount or coupon-code field shown when no usable promotion exists.
Remove or hide the field in that state so shoppers are not prompted to interrupt checkout and search externally for a code.
If a promotion is active, ensure the field and promotional messaging align with a real, redeemable offer.
Pair this work with relevant cart reassurance, such as clearly presented trust or policy information, but track the changes separately where feasible.
Compare downstream checkout completion and revenue per visitor before and after the change; do not credit a combined cart redesign to the coupon-field removal alone.
caveats: The source gives coupon hunting as a behavioral rationale, not a measured causal result.
Its reported monthly-revenue example reflects a combined cart package that also included a trust-policy bar; it cannot be attributed to this single change.

cards.title: Merchandise bestsellers in the mega-menu
cards.summary: Add a bestseller carousel to broad-catalog navigation to use popularity cues for product discovery, then verify that added interest becomes purchases.
cards.use_when: Improving navigation and category discovery for a store with enough assortment that shoppers may not know where to start.
steps: Identify genuinely high-selling products using a defined recent sales period and ensure selected items are in stock and commercially appropriate to feature.
Add a bestseller carousel to the mega-menu so shoppers can discover products others are purchasing while navigating categories.
Label the module clearly as bestseller or popular items so the social-proof cue is explicit rather than implied.
Track carousel exposure, product-page entries, add-to-cart rate, purchase rate, and category-level revenue to see whether navigation attention translates to commercial value.
Review the list periodically so it does not feature unavailable, seasonal, or stale products.
caveats: The source suggests shoppers responded with FOMO but does not establish that the response produced incremental purchases.
It does not define bestseller selection logic, inventory rules, or placement specifications.

cards.title: Combine quantitative and qualitative research into test hypotheses
cards.summary: Use funnel and heatmap evidence to locate shopper friction, then surveys and interviews to explain it before choosing a page or offer change.
cards.use_when: Creating a prioritized CRO backlog for a PDP, cart, checkout, or paid-traffic landing page instead of redesigning from preference.
steps: Use quantitative evidence first: review funnel drop-off and heatmaps to identify where shoppers hesitate, fail to progress, or never encounter important content.
Collect qualitative evidence next through post-purchase surveys, customer interviews, or usability sessions. Ask shoppers what made them buy and what nearly stopped them.
Join the two signals into a mechanism-led hypothesis. For example, if visitors do not reach a guarantee section and respondents express risk concerns, test a more visible reassurance treatment.
Write the proposed change, affected page, audience, primary metric, and expected shopper behavior before implementation.
Prioritize hypotheses only after research is complete, so the team is not merely optimizing the easiest visible page element.
caveats: The source gives illustrative tools and examples but no sample-size or interview-protocol requirements.
A below-the-fold guarantee issue is an example, not evidence that every store should move guarantee content upward.

cards.title: Use post-purchase surveys to capture motivations and objections
cards.summary: Ask purchasers what drove the purchase and what almost stopped it, then use their language to improve PDP, cart, checkout, and landing-page decisions.
cards.use_when: Setting up voice-of-customer research to improve a store's shopper journey and repeatable CRO hypothesis pipeline.
steps: Implement a post-purchase survey in the purchase flow or follow-up communication, using the current capabilities of the chosen survey tool.
Ask two core questions: what made the shopper purchase today, and what almost stopped them from buying today.
Classify answers into purchase motivations, objections, unanswered questions, trust concerns, and experience friction.
Review responses on a regular operating cadence and preserve the exact customer language for product-page copy, landing-page angles, offer framing, and checkout reassurance.
Cross-check recurring comments with funnel and behavioral data before making a change, then monitor whether the objection declines after the revised experience is live.
caveats: The source strongly prioritizes this practice but does not provide a survey timing, placement, response-rate target, or named current tool recommendation.
Post-purchase respondents exclude non-buyers, so use usability testing or on-site research when investigating abandonment by visitors who did not purchase.

cards.title: Convert recurring purchase objections into on-page reassurance
cards.summary: Turn repeated “almost did not buy” responses into clear, evidence-supported copy placed where shoppers make the purchase decision.
cards.use_when: Survey research shows recurring uncertainty that the PDP, landing page, cart, or checkout does not address.
steps: Review post-purchase answers for a recurring, specific objection rather than acting on a single anecdote.

Translate the objection into a clear reassurance or expectation-setting statement. The source example concerns uncertainty about how long results take, which could lead to prominently explaining the expected timeline.
Place the information close to the decision point: above the fold, by add to cart, in product details, or alongside the relevant offer or checkout step.
Ensure performance, outcome, delivery, or guarantee claims are accurate and supportable before publishing them.
Measure purchase conversion, revenue per visitor, and the recurrence of the objection in later survey responses to determine whether the treatment resolved the uncertainty.
caveats: The source provides an example but no formal method for ranking objections or validating claims.
Do not make outcome or timing claims simply because shoppers ask for them; product and legal substantiation still apply.

cards.title: Use a one-time customer survey to bootstrap research
cards.summary: When ongoing post-purchase research is absent, survey past purchasers and VIPs with a modest incentive to rapidly generate customer insight for ecommerce decisions.
cards.use_when: Launching initial customer research while a permanent post-purchase survey program is still being implemented.
steps: Create a short survey with a current form tool and send it to appropriate past customers or VIP segments.
Ask decision-relevant questions about why customers chose the product, what concerns they had, what was unclear, and what they value about the product or shopping experience.
If using an incentive such as a prize draw, make its terms, eligibility, and privacy treatment clear and verify applicable rules before sending.
Analyze answers for repeated themes, then turn those themes into hypotheses for PDP copy, offers, shipping reassurance, product education, or landing-page positioning.
Use the one-time study as an interim input, not a replacement for always-on post-purchase feedback.
caveats: The source mentions a Typeform-style survey and a $250 gift-card incentive as an example, not a required tool or amount.
Incentives can skew who responds and how they respond; interpret results alongside behavioral data and customer interviews.

cards.title: Run usability tests and customer interviews for purchase-friction insight
cards.summary: Observe people using the storefront and speak with purchasers to uncover clarity, navigation, and confidence issues that analytics alone cannot explain.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing why shoppers struggle on a PDP, cart, checkout, product quiz, or landing page after analytics identifies a possible drop-off point.
steps: Recruit relevant users to complete realistic shopping tasks on the store, such as finding a product, understanding its suitability, adding it to cart, and reaching checkout.
Observe where they hesitate, what they misinterpret, and what information they search for; do not coach them through the flow.
Interview customers directly where possible. Ask why they purchased, whether the purchase experience was clear, and what information or step was confusing.
Capture the customer's wording and map each issue to a specific journey stage and proposed change.
Compare recurring qualitative findings with heatmaps, funnel data, and survey themes before prioritizing a redesign or test.
caveats: The source does not prescribe recruiting criteria, sample size, incentives, recording consent, or interview cadence.
Customer interviews explain purchaser experiences but may not fully represent visitors who abandoned before purchase.

cards.title: Make revenue per visitor the primary CRO metric
cards.summary: Use revenue per visitor or session to evaluate ecommerce tests because it captures the combined effect of purchase conversion and average order value.
cards.use_when: Selecting the main success metric for PDP, landing-page, cart, checkout, pricing, bundle, or offer experiments.
steps: Set revenue per visitor or revenue per session as the primary outcome for most CRO tests, while retaining purchase conversion, average order value, and margin as diagnostic measures.
Use the metric to avoid false conversion-rate wins. For example, a large price cut may increase purchase conversion while reducing revenue per visitor.
For offer, bundle, and pricing tests, also inspect gross margin and contribution economics, since revenue per visitor alone may not establish profitability.
Report the test's effect by variant, traffic source, and relevant journey stage, rather than conflating email, returning customers, and cold paid traffic.
Use incremental gains from retained winners as the program's long-term output rather than overvaluing a single conversion-rate movement.
caveats: The source describes revenue per visitor as combining conversion rate and average order value but does not provide a formula or universal target.
Revenue is not profit; margin-sensitive decisions need an additional profitability check.

cards.title: Set AB-test duration for weekday and external-event coverage
cards.summary: Run adequately powered tests across repeated weekdays and avoid killing variants after a short-term event creates a misleading result.
cards.use_when: Scheduling and interpreting AB tests on high-enough-traffic ecommerce pages such as landing pages, PDPs, cart, or checkout.
steps: Calculate the sample required for the decision before launch, then estimate the duration needed to reach it.
Use the source's two-to-four-week planning range as a directional guideline and, for comprehensive higher-volume testing, run at least two weeks when feasible.
Ensure both variants experience repeated weekdays—for example, multiple Mondays through Thursdays—so normal day-of-week variation is represented.
Do not stop solely because one day is weak. Competitor promotions, campaigns, and other temporary factors can create misleading short-term movement.
If running concurrent experiments, separate them by journey area or page region, such as a homepage test and a cart test, and assess whether shopper overlap could still create interaction effects.
caveats: The source's duration guidance is not a replacement for a real sample-size calculation.
The source does not define how far apart concurrent tests must be or how to model interaction effects.

cards.title: Require statistical power before acting on a test
cards.summary: Plan the sample size and duration required to detect a meaningful ecommerce effect, and switch to larger concepts when traffic cannot support a micro-test.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether a PDP, landing-page, cart, checkout, or offer test can produce an actionable result.
steps: Define the primary business metric, baseline performance, minimum effect worth detecting, and practical decision deadline before launching the experiment.
Calculate the required sample size and planned duration using an appropriate current statistical method or testing platform; do not infer adequacy from a few early conversions.
Keep the test running through the planned coverage unless there is a valid operational reason to stop, rather than reacting to one poor day.
Check that traffic allocation, tracking, and variant exposure are working as intended before interpreting results.

If the required sample is unattainable, do not pretend an underpowered micro-test is conclusive. Test a larger research-led concept, improve traffic volume, or use qualitative evidence to guide a non-experimental change.
caveats: The source requires statistical power but does not supply a power-calculation method, significance threshold, or minimum detectable effect.
A statistically detectable change may still be commercially insignificant; assess revenue and margin impact.

cards.title: Map purchase-funnel drop-off before selecting a fix
cards.summary: Trace shopper progression from ad or entry page through PDP, cart, checkout, purchase, and post-purchase offers, then investigate why the largest relevant drop-off occurs.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing a weak purchase journey, especially when paid traffic currently lands directly on product pages.
steps: Map the store's actual path from traffic source to entry page, product page, cart, checkout, thank-you page, and any post-purchase upsell.
Review where shoppers fail to progress, using the funnel as a way to identify the stage requiring attention rather than as proof of its cause.

At lower traffic, the source suggests a full analytics implementation is not always necessary, but a basic drop-off review still is; collect enough data to avoid making decisions from a single anomalous day.
Use heatmaps, usability tests, post-purchase survey responses, and interviews to determine why the relevant stage may be failing.
Select a change that addresses the identified mechanism, then measure its effect on downstream purchase and revenue per visitor rather than only the immediate click.
caveats: The source does not name tools, exact funnel events, or a universal data-collection period; its one-to-two-week suggestion is directional.
A high drop-off rate alone does not reveal whether the issue is traffic quality, product fit, price, clarity, trust, or technical friction.

cards.title: Prioritize a CRO backlog with the PXL framework
cards.summary: After completing research, use the PXL prioritization framework to sequence ecommerce hypotheses instead of building tests in the order ideas arrive.
cards.use_when: Turning audit, analytics, survey, interview, and usability findings into an ordered roadmap for PDP, landing-page, cart, or checkout improvements.
steps: Complete the research stage first: audits, quantitative analysis, surveys, user tests, and customer interviews should supply the hypotheses to rank.
Create a backlog in which each item describes the shopper problem, proposed change, affected journey stage, expected outcome, evidence, and primary metric.
Apply the PXL framework consistently to score and sequence the backlog rather than prioritizing by stakeholder preference or implementation convenience alone.
Build the highest-priority viable hypotheses first, recording the result and learning so future prioritization improves.
Consult the framework's original, current documentation for the scoring mechanics instead of inventing what the acronym means.
caveats: The source explicitly does not claim ownership of PXL and does not provide its formula or individual scoring criteria.
A prioritization score supports judgment; it does not replace test feasibility, technical constraints, inventory realities, or margin considerations.

cards.title: Treat retained CRO winners as cumulative gains
cards.summary: A structured program compounds when validated winners remain implemented and losses are removed, so evaluate progress as accumulated revenue-per-visitor improvement over time.
cards.use_when: Reviewing ongoing CRO investment and deciding how to report the value of a testing program to ecommerce stakeholders.
steps: Maintain a test log with the hypothesis, page or journey stage, audience, result, implementation decision, and primary revenue-per-visitor impact.
Implement validated winners and remove losing variants so retained improvements become the baseline for the next round of optimization.
Report cumulative performance over months and years alongside individual test outcomes, emphasizing the aggregate effect of improvements that remain live.
Avoid treating a program as unsuccessful merely because one isolated win is modest; comprehensive research, prioritization, and repeated experiments are intended to create an accumulating system.
Review older implemented winners periodically if catalog, traffic mix, pricing, seasonality, or customer expectations have materially changed.
caveats: The source's claim that winners outweigh losses by an extreme margin is rhetorical and does not establish a measured universal win rate or compounding multiplier.
Compounding depends on accurate measurement, valid decisions, and keeping winners appropriate as business conditions change.

Ask why they purchased, whether the purchase experience was clear, and what information or step was confusing.","Capture the customer's wording and map each issue to a specific journey stage and proposed change.","Compare recurring qualitative findings with heatmaps, funnel data, and survey themes before prioritizing a redesign or test."],"caveats":["The source does not prescribe recruiting criteria, sample size, incentives, recording consent, or interview cadence.","Customer interviews explain purchaser experiences but may not fully represent visitors who abandoned before purchase."],"tags":["testing","user-testing","customer-research","usability","interviews","checkout","product-page"]},{"title":"Make revenue per visitor the primary CRO metric","summary":"Use revenue per visitor or session to evaluate ecommerce tests because it captures the combined effect of purchase conversion and average order value.","use_when":"Selecting the main success metric for PDP, landing-page, cart, checkout, pricing, bundle, or offer experiments.","steps":["Set revenue per visitor or revenue per session as the primary outcome for most CRO tests, while retaining purchase conversion, average order value, and margin as diagnostic measures.","Use the metric to avoid false conversion-rate wins. For example, a large price cut may increase purchase conversion while reducing revenue per visitor.","For offer, bundle, and pricing tests, also inspect gross margin and contribution economics, since revenue per visitor alone may not establish profitability.","Report the test's effect by variant, traffic source, and relevant journey stage, rather than conflating email, returning customers, and cold paid traffic.","Use incremental gains from retained winners as the program's long-term output rather than overvaluing a single conversion-rate movement."],"caveats":["The source describes revenue per visitor as combining conversion rate and average order value but does not provide a formula or universal target.","Revenue is not profit; margin-sensitive decisions need an additional profitability check."],"tags":["testing","measurement","revenue-per-visitor","average-order-value","pricing","conversion-optimization","metrics"]},{"title":"Set AB-test duration for weekday and external-event coverage","summary":"Run adequately powered tests across repeated weekdays and avoid killing variants after a short-term event creates a misleading result.","use_when":"Scheduling and interpreting AB tests on high-enough-traffic ecommerce pages such as landing pages, PDPs, cart, or checkout.","steps":["Calculate the sample required for the decision before launch, then estimate the duration needed to reach it.","Use the source's two-to-four-week planning range as a directional guideline and, for comprehensive higher-volume testing, run at least two weeks when feasible.","Ensure both variants experience repeated weekdays—for example, multiple Mondays through Thursdays—so normal day-of-week variation is represented.","Do not stop solely because one day is weak. input.source_name: Conversion Rate Optimization Framework Revealed - Step By Step Breakdown.docx

cards.title: Choose CRO strategy by monthly session volume
cards.summary: Split CRO approach: big swings under 300,000 monthly sessions, comprehensive AB testing above it.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to allocate CRO effort for a store based on traffic and order volume
steps: Pull monthly session volume from your analytics and compare it to the roughly 300,000 sessions/month line used as the decision point.

Under that line, default to big swings rather than micro-tests: full landing page design concepts, PDP redesigns based on data, and offer/price tests. Comprehensive CRO (long audits, deep quantitative and qualitative research, isolated AB tests) is not worth the overhead at low volume.

Above that line, with a decent conversion rate and enough orders to quantify results, run comprehensive full CRO: AB testing, data analysis, long audits and deep data work. At this level comprehensive CRO remains the most powerful lever for growing revenue per visitor.

Treat the threshold as a moving internal benchmark rather than a fixed law — the source notes it changed within roughly the last six to twelve months — and re-check whether your data volume is actually sufficient before committing to an AB testing program.
caveats: The source does not define what counts as a 'good enough' conversion rate or 'enough orders' above the threshold.
300,000 monthly sessions is a heuristic benchmark, not a validated industry constant.

cards.title: Run big swings instead of micro-tests on small stores
cards.summary: Low-traffic stores should redesign PDPs, test offers and build landing pages instead of testing button colors.
cards.use_when: Planning the CRO roadmap for a store with limited traffic that cannot power small element tests
steps: Stop allocating testing capacity to small PDP elements such as button color, above-fold image swaps or small copy snippets — at low volume these rarely reach significance and rarely move revenue.
Instead do PDP redesigns driven by data, and treat the 'based on data' part as mandatory: the redesign should follow from funnel, survey, interview or heatmap findings rather than taste.
Layer in landing page design concepts, since pre-sell pages carry the biggest uplift for stores under the volume threshold, and run offer/price experiments monthly.

Expect the model to work differently when cost per click is high: scaling ad spend or refreshing creative may lift conversion little, whereas bigger on-site swings can produce a step change in conversion rate or revenue per session.
caveats: The source gives no specification for what a data-driven PDP redesign should change.
'Can literally double conversion or revenue per session' is a rhetorical claim without baseline, sample size or test period.

cards.title: Insert a landing page between ad click and money pages
cards.summary: Put a pre-sell landing page between the ad and product or collection pages instead of sending traffic straight to the store.
cards.use_when: Paid traffic is being routed directly to PDPs, homepages or collection pages and performance is flat
steps: Stop sending paid clicks straight to product pages, homepages, or collection pages — the source treats that as leaving money on the table.
Add an intermediate step: a dedicated landing page that visitors hit first and that pre-sells them before they continue to the product or collection ('money') pages.

Design that page as a concept with a defined angle and offer, because landing page design concepts are counted among the big swings available to stores under the traffic threshold, and the source reports landing pages have the biggest uplift for those stores.
Once the page is live, measure its contribution in revenue per visitor and use it as a lever to scale cold traffic rather than judging it purely on click-through.
caveats: The source does not specify landing page format, length, or offer structure.
One reported example — about 20k per month on cold traffic with the ability to scale — is a case illustration, not a benchmark; the currency and period are not stated.

cards.title: Test offers and price points on a monthly cadence
cards.summary: Run month-to-month offer experiments: BOGO, three-for-two, build-a-bundle pages, and different price points.
cards.use_when: Looking for revenue-per-visitor gains that do not depend on design changes or page-level test traffic
steps: Set a monthly cadence for offer experiments rather than treating offers as a permanent setting.
Test structures such as buy one get one free, three for the price of two, and build-a-bundle pages.
Test different price points directly — the source lists price testing alongside offer testing as something that moves the needle.
Because offer changes can shift both conversion rate and average order value, evaluate them on revenue per visitor or revenue per session rather than conversion rate alone.
Keep the offer tests distinct from layout tests so you can attribute the revenue effect, and note that offer work is typically easier to power than small page-element tests at low traffic.
caveats: The source does not state test duration, sample size, or a decision rule for declaring an offer winner.
'Three for the power of two' appears in the source material and is likely a transcription artifact for three for the price of two.

cards.title: Remove the discount code box when no promotion is active
cards.summary: An empty discount field on the cart drives coupon-hunting abandonment; remove it unless discounts are live.
cards.use_when: Auditing cart or coupon page design on a store with no active promotions
steps: Check whether a discount or coupon code field is present on the cart or coupon page while no promotion is running.
If nothing is active, remove the field. An empty box invites shoppers to leave the site to search for a code, which breaks the purchase flow and frequently ends in abandonment.
Pair the removal with other cart-level trust elements such as a trust policy bar, which the source groups into the same cart optimization package.
Measure the change on revenue per visitor, not conversion rate alone, and keep the field out until there is a real promotion to justify it.
caveats: Coupon-hunting abandonment is given as the rationale, not as a measured outcome in the source.

A reported result of about $40,000 in monthly revenue is attributed to the combined cart optimization (discount box removal plus trust policy bar), not to either change alone; currency and period are not stated.

cards.title: Use bestseller carousels in the mega-menu to create FOMO
cards.summary: Surface bestsellers in the mega-menu so shoppers see what other people are buying.
cards.use_when: Optimizing site navigation and category discovery for a store with a broad catalog
steps: Add a bestseller carousel into the mega-menu so products other shoppers are buying are visible during navigation.
The mechanism is social proof and scarcity of attention: the source reports more shoppers reacting with FOMO toward products flagged as popular once the carousel was added.
Treat the carousel as one of the larger structural changes rather than a micro-test, since it changes how visitors are routed into the catalog.
Evaluate the effect at the level of product and category entry, watching whether interest translates into purchases rather than only clicks.
caveats: The source does not specify selection criteria for bestsellers or rules for placing the carousel.
It does not confirm that the observed FOMO translated into purchases versus interest or clicking only.

cards.title: Pair quantitative and qualitative data to form test hypotheses
cards.summary: Use heatmaps and funnel drop-off to find what is broken, then surveys and interviews to find why.
cards.use_when: Building a prioritized test hypothesis backlog instead of guessing at changes
steps: Start with quantitative instruments — heatmaps and funnel drop-off analysis — to locate what is happening. A typical finding is that users never see a below-the-fold trust or guarantee section.
Then run qualitative research — post-purchase surveys and customer interviews — to discover why. For example, ask what almost stopped someone from buying today.
Combine both signals into hypotheses before designing tests, so the test is aimed at a mechanism rather than a surface element.
Do not skip either half: numbers tell you where to look, customer language tells you what to change and how to phrase it.
caveats: No specific heatmap or funnel tooling is prescribed, and the 'users missing below-the-fold guarantees' case is illustrative rather than a completion criterion.
No sample size or interview protocol is given.

cards.title: Ask the two core post-purchase survey questions
cards.summary: Set up post-purchase surveys and always ask what made them purchase and what almost stopped them.
cards.use_when: Setting up or auditing survey instrumentation on any store
steps: Ensure a post-purchase survey is live. The source treats this as non-negotiable and the single most effective optimization lever, so if it does not exist, set it up before other work.
Ask at least two questions: 'What made you purchase today?' and 'What made you almost not purchase today?' (a close variant in the source wording is 'what almost stopped you from buying today?').
Treat the first question as a source of purchase motivations — for example, a customer buying because they want to lose weight — and the second as a source of objections and friction.
Review answers regularly and route them into copy, angle and layout decisions rather than filing them as reporting.
caveats: No survey timing or placement (page, email, widget) is specified.
The tool named in the source material is transcription-ambiguous and should be verified against current options rather than treated as a fixed recommendation.

cards.title: Turn 'almost didn't buy' answers into front-end copy changes
cards.summary: Use objections surfaced by post-purchase surveys to rewrite the copy or angle on the front end of the site.
cards.use_when: Survey responses reveal recurring uncertainties that are not addressed on the page
steps: Mine the second survey question for concrete objections. A recurring example: customers did not know how long it would take to see results.
Convert the objection into an explicit claim on the front end — for instance, telling visitors they will see noticeable results in the first six weeks.
Place that language where the objection arises: above the fold, near the add-to-cart, or in the PDP copy that frames the offer.
Re-survey after the change to check whether the objection stops appearing, and treat the change as a big swing rather than a word-level test.
caveats: The source gives one worked example but no process for selecting which answers to act on or how to rank objections.

cards.title: Run a one-time survey when no post-purchase survey exists
cards.summary: Email VIPs and customers a one-time Typeform-style survey with a gift-card incentive to collect feedback fast.
cards.use_when: You need customer insight but no post-purchase survey is instrumented yet
steps: Stand up a one-time survey using a form tool such as Typeform, aimed at your list of VIPs and past customers.
Ask the questions that matter for feedback on the product and store rather than generic satisfaction items.
Offer a chance to win a $250 Amazon gift card as the participation incentive.
Use the responses as input to hypotheses and copy changes while the permanent post-purchase survey is being set up.
caveats: The exact tool and incentive terms should be verified before use; they are not fixed requirements.
Incentivized one-time surveys can bias responses toward incentive-motivated participants.

cards.title: Run user testing and phone interviews with customers
cards.summary: Watch users on the site and call customers to ask why they bought and what was unclear.
cards.use_when: You need qualitative depth beyond survey answers, especially on usability problems
steps: Recruit people to go onto your site and survey them, then run proper usability tests and user interviews to surface friction.

In parallel, call customers directly. The described practice is to phone customers and quiz them with questions like: why did you purchase, did you have a good purchasing experience, and was anything unclear?
Record the language customers use about clarity and hesitation, and feed it back into hypotheses and copy.
Treat this as an ongoing practice rather than a one-off project, since it produces the 'why' that heatmaps and funnels cannot.
caveats: No sample size, cadence or screening criteria are given for user tests or customer calls.

cards.title: Make revenue per visitor the primary CRO metric
cards.summary: Optimize revenue per visitor or per session rather than raw conversion rate, because it blends conversion rate and average order value.
cards.use_when: Choosing the headline metric for a test program or reporting CRO results to stakeholders
steps: Report and optimize revenue per visitor (or revenue per session) as the primary metric; the source recommends focusing on it roughly nine times out of ten.
Use it because it combines conversion rate and average order value, so it prevents wins on one dimension from being paid for by losses on the other.
Watch it expose false wins: slashing prices can lift conversion rate dramatically while the brand makes less per visitor, so a conversion-rate-only dashboard would celebrate a revenue-losing change.
In comprehensive programs, look for isolated AB tests that produce incremental increases in revenue per visitor and treat those increments as the compounding output of the program.
caveats: The source describes revenue per visitor as a blend of conversion rate and average order value but gives no calculation formula and no target level.
It does not specify what to do in the remaining one-out-of-ten cases where another metric may lead.

cards.title: Run tests long enough to survive external factors
cards.summary: Test for two to four weeks and cover repeated weekdays so competitor sales and day effects don't kill winners.
cards.use_when: Setting test duration and scheduling for anyone running AB tests
steps: Plan around a two-to-four-week window rather than stopping early; external factors such as a competitor's sale on a single day can push a test down and trigger a rash decision to kill a potentially winning variant.
For comprehensive tests on stores above the traffic threshold, run for at least two weeks so external factors do not distort the result.
Use a repeated-weekday schedule — for example two Mondays, two Tuesdays, two Wednesdays and two Thursdays — so day-of-week effects are balanced across variants.
When running concurrent tests, separate them by area: a homepage test and a cart test can run together because they are far apart, as can an above-fold test with a below-fold test.
caveats: The two-week minimum is stated for comprehensive tests above the traffic threshold; the source does not say whether it replaces the broader two-to-four-week guidance.
The repeated-weekday schedule is given as an example, not as a mandatory rule, and the source does not define how 'far apart' concurrent tests must be.

cards.title: Ensure statistical power before trusting a test
cards.summary: Design tests with adequate statistical power rather than reading early or underpowered results.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether a test result is actionable, especially on mid-volume stores
steps: Treat statistical power as a design parameter: decide required sample size and duration up front so the test can detect the effect size you care about.
Do not stop a test on the basis of a bad day or two — the source explicitly warns that external events can make a test look like a loser while it is still a potential winner.
Combine the power requirement with the two-to-four-week duration guidance so you have both enough sessions and enough weekday coverage.
If volume is too low to power a small test at all, that is a signal to run a bigger structural swing instead of a micro-test.
caveats: The source does not give a method for calculating or achieving statistical power, nor any significance threshold.

cards.title: Map funnel drop-off through PDP, cart, checkout and post-purchase
cards.summary: Analyze where people drop off through the funnel — and analyze why — without necessarily running full analytics software.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing a store where traffic flows straight from ad to product page
steps: Look at which funnel step people are dropping off at as a baseline practice; full Google Analytics or tracking-software analysis is not required below the low-traffic threshold, but the drop-off review is.
If traffic goes straight from ad to PDP, walk the sequence explicitly: product page, cart, checkout, thank-you page, and the post-purchase upsell step if your stack supports one.
For each drop-off point, follow the count with a cause analysis — this is where heatmaps and customer interviews take over from funnel numbers.
Allow roughly one to two weeks of data collection before making decisions at low volume, so the drop-off picture is stable enough to act on.
caveats: The period for the traffic threshold is not stated in the excerpt; treat the threshold as approximate.
The source does not name specific analytics tools or metrics for the funnel review.

cards.title: Prioritize research findings with the PXL framework
cards.summary: After completing research, score and sequence hypotheses using the PXL framework rather than intuition.
cards.use_when: Turning a pile of audit, survey and analytics findings into an ordered test backlog
steps: Finish the research phase first — audit, quantitative analysis, user testing, surveys — before scoring anything.
Then build a prioritization framework using the PXL framework. The source is explicit that this framework is not theirs and does not claim to have invented it.
Use the framework to rank hypotheses so the highest-potential changes get built and run first, rather than testing in the order findings arrived.
Keep the framework applied consistently, since the compounding value of a CRO program depends on sequencing the right tests rather than running more of them.
caveats: The source does not state what PXL stands for or provide the exact scoring structure or formula.
Reproducing the framework requires consulting its original source rather than guessing at the acronym.

cards.title: Expect winning tests to compound, not just outweigh losers
cards.summary: Wins beat losses by a large margin and their revenue-per-visitor gains stack month over month and year over year.
cards.use_when: Justifying continued investment in a structured testing program
steps: Frame the program around accumulated incremental revenue per visitor rather than a single test's headline result.
Recognize that a high win-to-loss ratio means implemented wins persist on the site while losing variants disappear, so gains stack on top of each other.
Plan for the compounding to show up month on month and year on year as more winners are implemented and left in place.

Use this framing when the immediate result of a program looks modest — comprehensive audits, isolated AB tests and incremental revenue-per-visitor gains are the building blocks, not the whole outcome.
caveats: The claim that winners outweigh losers 'times 100' is rhetorical; the source does not quantify the compounding effect or provide a measured multiplier.
